Read in the data.¶

The parse_dates argument converts to a pandas datetime object. Note that below we set "date" as the index. Thus "date" is no longer a column name.

In [4]:
df = pd.read_csv("../../data/CTA_-_Ridership_-_Daily_Boarding_Totals_20240731.csv", parse_dates=["service_date"])

df.columns = ["date", "day_type", "bus", "rail", "total"]  # shorter names
df = df.sort_values("date").set_index("date")
df = df.drop("total", axis=1)  # no need for total, it's just bus + rail
df = df.drop_duplicates()  # remove duplicated months (2011-10 and 2014-07)

Differencing¶

Differencing is a technique used on seasonal and trended data. You can see there is the weekly periodicity- the diff removes the periodicity. Compare with for example, diff(5). One can also decompose time series into seasonal (one or more) and trend components. See for example Forecasting Principles and Practice (fpp3) Chapter 3.

Below, the dotted plots on the top plot show the 7-day shifted values. You can see where the differenced values on the bottom plot are close to zero.

In [31]:
diff_7 = df[["bus", "rail"]].diff(7)["2024-01":"2024-03"]

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(8, 5))
df.plot(ax=axs[0], legend=False, marker=".")  # original time series
df.shift(7).plot(ax=axs[0], grid=True, legend=False, linestyle=":")  # lagged
diff_7.plot(ax=axs[1], grid=True, marker=".")  # 7-day difference time series
axs[0].set_ylim([80_000, 610_000])  # extra code – beautifies the plot
plt.show()

We can see a few places where the differences were large, for example near Jan 15. We might check that day

Now let's look at the yearly seasonality and the long-term trends. You can see that, as of the beginning of 2024, ridership seemed to be reboundingto pre pandemic levels.

We can also see yearly seasonality, as well as some trending.

In [54]:
period = slice("2001", "2024")
df_monthly = df[["bus", "rail"]].resample('ME').mean()  # compute the mean for each month
rolling_average_12_months = df_monthly[period].rolling(window=12).mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
df_monthly[period].plot(ax=ax, marker=".")

We can do seasonal-yearly- differencing here, which removes the trending- asisd from pandemic craziness.

In [55]:
df_monthly.diff(12)[period].plot(grid=True, marker=".", figsize=(8, 3))

plt.show()

ARIMA models¶

We use statsmodels library. You will need to install this. As we have seen, the ARIMA model is auto-regressive integrated moving average model. It and exponential smoothing are the two most widely used time series modeling approaches. See fpp3 Chapters 9 and 8; respectively.

The model below is an autoregressive (AR) model with seasonal components that is modeled as moving average (MA), and with seasonal differencing of 7. Seasonal ARIMA models are also reffered to as SARIMA. We just consider the rail data.

Notice we pass the data to the model at construction, rather than at fit, as in sklearn and keras. See Geron, and also the statsmodels docs

In [ ]:
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA

origin, today = "2023-01-01", "2023-05-31" ## pick a several weeks time period
rail_series = df.loc[origin:today]["rail"].asfreq("D") # "D" gives daily as freq
model = ARIMA(rail_series,
              order=(1, 0, 0), ## in fact this model is an AR only model.
              seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 7)) # seasonal model orders and differencing.

model = model.fit()
y_pred = model.forecast()

We may have gotten lucky above with the day. Below we train a new model each day and find mean absolute error. This is just to see how well the one day arima forecast does on average.

In [75]:
origin, start_date, end_date = "2023-01-01", "2023-03-01", "2023-05-31"
time_period = pd.date_range(start_date, end_date)
rail_series = df.loc[origin:end_date]["rail"].asfreq("D")
y_preds = []
for today in time_period.shift(-1):
    model = ARIMA(rail_series[origin:today],  # train on data up to "today"
                  order=(1, 0, 0),
                  seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 7))
    model = model.fit()  # note that we retrain the model every day!
    y_pred = model.forecast().iloc[0]
    y_preds.append(y_pred)

y_preds = pd.Series(y_preds, index=time_period)
mae = (y_preds - rail_series[time_period]).abs().mean()
mae
Out[75]:
19135.61164006469

So we did get lucky. Still not terribly bad. We can compare true and model predictions

plt.show()

We can revise the code to give predictions seven days ahead, and plot.

In [92]:
y_preds = []
for today in time_period.shift(-1):
    model = ARIMA(rail_series[origin:today],  # train on data up to "today"
                  order=(1, 0, 0),
                  seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 7))
    model = model.fit()  # note that we retrain the model every day!
    y_pred = model.forecast(steps = 7).iloc[6]
    y_preds.append(y_pred)

y_preds = pd.Series(y_preds, index=time_period)
In [93]:
# Shift the predictions by 7 days to align with the actual values
y_preds_shifted = y_preds.shift(7)

# Plot the actual values and the shifted predictions
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
rail_series.loc[time_period].plot(label="True", ax=ax, marker=".", grid=True)
ax.plot(y_preds_shifted, color="r", marker=".", label="SARIMA Forecasts")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Autocorrelation.¶

Describes the correlations between lagged values; that is, time series with itself, at different lagged values. An assumption is that the correlations only depend on the lag, and not where along the time series you are. Such time series are said to be stationary. See fpp3 Section 2.8 (though stationarity is not mentioned until Ch. 7).

Below you can clearly see the weekly seasonality evidenced by large correlations at multiples of 7.

Stationarity is a desireable property for statistical modeling that is usually violated.

In [ ]:
# extra code – shows how to plot the Autocorrelation Function (ACF) and the
#              Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)

from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf, plot_pacf

fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows=1, ncols=2, figsize=(15, 5))
plot_acf(df[period]["rail"], ax=axs[0], lags=35)
axs[0].grid()
plot_pacf(df[period]["rail"], ax=axs[1], lags=35, method="ywm")
axs[1].grid()
plt.show()

A Simple RNN model¶

First consider just the time series without any features. Later we will use day_type as a predictor.

Split the time series into three periods, for training, validation and testing.

Below is analogous to what Chollet is doing in Ch. 10 code, except note here that there are no predictors- these data sets only contain rail. We are using the sequence to forecast itself. In Chollet, there are predictors in addition to the target. Later we incorporate predictors.

In [ ]:
import tensorflow as tf

rail_train = df["rail"]["2021-01":"2023-6"] / 1e6
rail_valid = df["rail"]["2023-7":"2023-12"] / 1e6
rail_test = df["rail"]["2024-01":] / 1e6
In [ ]:
seq_length = 56
tf.random.set_seed(42)  # extra code – ensures reproducibility
train_ds = tf.keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array(
    rail_train.to_numpy(),
    targets=rail_train[seq_length:],
    sequence_length=seq_length,
    batch_size=32,
    shuffle=True,
    seed=42
)
valid_ds = tf.keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array(
    rail_valid.to_numpy(),
    targets=rail_valid[seq_length:],
    sequence_length=seq_length,
    batch_size=32
)

We define a convenience function.

In [ ]:
def fit_and_evaluate(model, train_set, valid_set, learning_rate, epochs=5):
    early_stopping_cb = tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(
        monitor="val_mae", patience=50, restore_best_weights=True)
    opt = tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=learning_rate, momentum=0.9)
    model.compile(loss=tf.keras.losses.Huber(), optimizer=opt, metrics=["mae"])
    history = model.fit(train_set, validation_data=valid_set, epochs=epochs,
                        callbacks=[early_stopping_cb])
    valid_loss, valid_mae = model.evaluate(valid_set)
    return valid_mae * 1e6
In [ ]:
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Input, SimpleRNN, Dense
from tensorflow.keras.models import Model


inputs = Input(shape=[None, 1])
x = SimpleRNN(32,  return_sequences=True, activation = "tanh")(inputs)
x = SimpleRNN(32,  return_sequences=True, activation="tanh")(x)
x = SimpleRNN(32, activation="tanh")(x)
outputs = Dense(1)(x)

model = Model(inputs, outputs)
In [ ]:
fit_and_evaluate(model, train_ds, valid_ds, learning_rate=0.02)

Multivariate time series¶

Here we use day_type and bus to predict rail

In [52]:
df_mulvar = df[["bus", "rail"]] / 1e6  # use both bus & rail series as input
df_mulvar["next_day_type"] = df["day_type"].shift(-1)  # we know tomorrow's type
df_mulvar = pd.get_dummies(df_mulvar, dtype = int)  # one-hot. You need the dtype = int!
In [50]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
ohc = OneHotEncoder()
day_enc = ohc.fit_transform(df[["day_type"]])
day_df = pd.DataFrame(day_enc.toarray(), columns = ohc.get_feature_names_out())

df_mulvar = pd.concat([df[["bus", "rail"]], day_df], axis = 1)

tf.random.set_seed(42)

seq_length = 56
train_multask_ds = tf.keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array(
    mulvar_train.to_numpy(),
    targets=mulvar_train[["bus", "rail"]][seq_length:],  # 2 targets per day
    sequence_length=seq_length,
    batch_size=32,
    shuffle=True,
    seed=42
)
valid_multask_ds = tf.keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array(
    mulvar_valid.to_numpy(),
    targets=mulvar_valid[["bus", "rail"]][seq_length:],
    sequence_length=seq_length,
    batch_size=32
)

Now let's create an RNN that predicts all 14 next values at once:

In [ ]:
tf.random.set_seed(42)  # extra code – ensures reproducibility

def split_inputs_and_targets(mulvar_series, ahead=14, target_col=1):
    return mulvar_series[:, :-ahead], mulvar_series[:, -ahead:, target_col]

ahead_train_ds = tf.keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array(
    mulvar_train.to_numpy(),
    targets=None,
    sequence_length=seq_length + 14,
    batch_size=32,
    shuffle=True,
    seed=42
).map(split_inputs_and_targets)
ahead_valid_ds = tf.keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array(
    mulvar_valid.to_numpy(),
    targets=None,
    sequence_length=seq_length + 14,
    batch_size=32
).map(split_inputs_and_targets)
In [ ]:
tf.random.set_seed(42)

ahead_model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.SimpleRNN(32, input_shape=[None, 5]),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(14)
])
In [ ]:
# extra code – compiles, fits, and evaluates the model, like earlier
fit_and_evaluate(ahead_model, ahead_train_ds, ahead_valid_ds,
                 learning_rate=0.02)

In [ ]:
X = mulvar_valid.to_numpy()[np.newaxis, :seq_length]  # shape [1, 56, 5]
Y_pred = ahead_model.predict(X)  # shape [1, 14]

Now let's create an RNN that predicts the next 14 steps at each time step. That is, instead of just forecasting time steps 56 to 69 based on time steps 0 to 55, it will forecast time steps 1 to 14 at time step 0, then time steps 2 to 15 at time step 1, and so on, and finally it will forecast time steps 56 to 69 at the last time step. Notice that the model is causal: when it makes predictions at any time step, it can only see past time steps.

To prepare the datasets, we can use to_windows() twice, to get sequences of consecutive windows, like this:

In [ ]:
my_series = tf.data.Dataset.range(7)
dataset = to_windows(to_windows(my_series, 3), 4)
list(dataset)
Out[ ]:
[<tf.Tensor: shape=(4, 3), dtype=int64, numpy=
 array([[0, 1, 2],
        [1, 2, 3],
        [2, 3, 4],
        [3, 4, 5]])>,
 <tf.Tensor: shape=(4, 3), dtype=int64, numpy=
 array([[1, 2, 3],
        [2, 3, 4],
        [3, 4, 5],
        [4, 5, 6]])>]

Then we can split these elements into the desired inputs and targets:

In [ ]:
dataset = dataset.map(lambda S: (S[:, 0], S[:, 1:]))
list(dataset)
Out[ ]:
[(<tf.Tensor: shape=(4,), dtype=int64, numpy=array([0, 1, 2, 3])>,
  <tf.Tensor: shape=(4, 2), dtype=int64, numpy=
  array([[1, 2],
         [2, 3],
         [3, 4],
         [4, 5]])>),
 (<tf.Tensor: shape=(4,), dtype=int64, numpy=array([1, 2, 3, 4])>,
  <tf.Tensor: shape=(4, 2), dtype=int64, numpy=
  array([[2, 3],
         [3, 4],
         [4, 5],
         [5, 6]])>)]

Let's wrap this idea into a utility function. It will also take care of shuffling (optional) and batching:

In [ ]:
def to_seq2seq_dataset(series, seq_length=56, ahead=14, target_col=1,
                       batch_size=32, shuffle=False, seed=None):
    ds = to_windows(tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices(series), ahead + 1)
    ds = to_windows(ds, seq_length).map(lambda S: (S[:, 0], S[:, 1:, 1]))
    if shuffle:
        ds = ds.shuffle(8 * batch_size, seed=seed)
    return ds.batch(batch_size)
In [ ]:
seq2seq_train = to_seq2seq_dataset(mulvar_train, shuffle=True, seed=42)
seq2seq_valid = to_seq2seq_dataset(mulvar_valid)
In [ ]:
tf.random.set_seed(42)  # extra code – ensures reproducibility
seq2seq_model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.SimpleRNN(32, return_sequences=True, input_shape=[None, 5]),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(14)
    # equivalent: tf.keras.layers.TimeDistributed(tf.keras.layers.Dense(14))
    # also equivalent: tf.keras.layers.Conv1D(14, kernel_size=1)
])
In [ ]:
fit_and_evaluate(seq2seq_model, seq2seq_train, seq2seq_valid,
                 learning_rate=0.1)
